## The project

Propagation Card Reader began as a practical problem at the **UBC Botanical Garden Nursery**:
there were decades of handwritten propagation cards holding hard-won horticultural
knowledge—such as sowing dates, treatments, successes, and failures—but no realistic way
to digitize them. Commercial OCR meant ongoing cloud costs and sending collection data
off-site, while manual entry required staff time the Garden simply didn't have.

The answer was to run a vision-language model locally. It is free, private, and adept enough
at parsing messy handwriting to be genuinely useful. This approach was highly effective 
because the knowledge on the cards utilizes a relatively restricted sublanguage, and portions
of the expected OCR output—specifically accession numbers and taxon name associations—are
already known and predictable.

## The author

Built by **Kevin Kubeck**, a horticulturist at UBC Botanical Garden with decades of propagation
and plant-collection experience, alongside a self-taught background in Python, data science, and
data tooling for conservation. 

The first two versions of this project were built independently. This final iteration utilized an
agentic coding workflow, leveraging Claude Opus 4.6 as an orchestrator and the local `openclaw`
system as a harness.

## Why local-first matters

For a botanical garden, collection data can be highly sensitive, especially when it involves
rare-species locations, provenance, and historical institutional records. Keeping the entire OCR
pipeline on local hardware ensures the garden never has to trade privacy or budget for the 
benefits of digitization. That principle is the core motivation behind this tool.
